VIDEO.title: The REAL Meaning Behind Jesus' Teaching on the EYE! (Matthew 6:19-34)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: You always end up finding what you're looking for.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 6:19-34: treasures in heaven, the eye as the lamp of the body, two masters, and do not worry: look at the birds and the lilies, and seek first His kingdom and His righteousness.
It looks like several separate messages, but Jesus is unpacking ideas that run through the whole sermon. The scene has not changed: disciples, with the crowds listening.
How can disciples live without worry when they have families and responsibilities? Jesus' answer: your heart (6:21) and your eye (6:22).

'If your eye is clear' reaches for a Hebrew idiom, the good eye (ayin tovah). God saw that what He made was good (Genesis 1). A good eye looks at people with complete love and sees beauty and potential, the way God called Gideon a mighty man of valor. 'He who is generous' in Proverbs 22:9 is literally 'good of eye.'

In the video's chiasm, 6:19-34 parallels the end of chapter 5: 'be perfect' (5:48) is answered here. How do I love completely like the Father? Have the Father's good eye. A bad eye looks for the bad and finds it, leading to fear, anxiety and worry.

The lesson: one key to fulfilling the sermon is to have God's good eye, and that takes trusting Him. The Pharisees had a bad eye and missed the kingdom in front of them. If the Lord has a good eye toward His creation and we mirror Him on earth as in heaven, so should we.
QUOTES: Your heart must be guarded carefully because of what is inside of it.
To have God's good eye is to look at the world, to look around at people, from the perspective of complete love.
You always end up finding what you're looking for.
If we have God's good eye, we will find the beauty and the potential that we seek in others, which is the key to giving love.
One of the keys to fulfilling the Sermon on the Mount and being God's kingdom spreaders is to have God's good eye.

method.h: Ask what holds the passage together
method.p: At first 6:19-34 looks like four separate sayings: treasure, the eye, two masters, worry. The teacher's question: what single idea joins them, and how do they connect back to chapter 5? Read the passage once looking for the word 'eye' and once looking for 'heart.'

LSB_QUOTES.text: for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
The eye is the lamp of the body; so then if your eye is clear, your whole body will be full of light.
But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

src.text: Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

lines.text: The earthly treasure is food, drink and clothes (6:25). All of it will disappear: moth, rust and thieves. Instead God's people focus on His kingdom and His righteousness, different from the righteousness of the religious leaders.

'Destroy' (aphanizō) is the same verb as the fasters who 'neglect their appearance' in 6:16. 'Rust' is literally 'eating' (brōsis). Luke adds: 'Sell your possessions and give it as charity' (Luke 12:33).

FOUR.title: The eye is the lamp of the body

src.text: The eye is the lamp of the body; so then if your eye is clear, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!

lines.text: My translation says 'healthy,' but Jesus is reaching for something very Jewish: the good eye. If your heart is wrong, your focus will be off; if your eye is not good, you'll end up serving what you should not.
'Clear' is haplous (G573): single, sincere. Its noun haplotēs means generosity: 'he who gives, with generosity' (Romans 12:8). 'Bad' is ponēros, 'evil,' as in the 'evil eye' of stinginess.

src.text: No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.

lines.text: The disciple faces a choice, and Jesus is the one forcing it. It all comes down to which eye you choose to have.
'Serve' is douleuō, to serve as a slave. 'Wealth' is mamōnas, an Aramaic word for money and property (older versions: 'mammon'). The evil eye 'hurries after wealth' (Proverbs 28:22).

FOUR.title: Look at the birds, observe the lilies

left.text: Look at the birds of the air, that they do not sow, nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?

right.text: Observe how the lilies of the field grow; they do not toil nor do they spin, yet I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory clothed himself like one of these.

lines.text: A bad eye looks for things to fear and mistrust, and finds them; that leads to anxiety, worry and loneliness. That is why Jesus moves from the eye straight to worry.
God 'gives to the animal its food, / And to the young ravens which call out' (Psalm 147:9). 'All flesh is grass' (Isaiah 40:6). The answer to worry is a priority: 'seek first His kingdom' (6:33).

FOUR.note: Chrysostom: 'For neither did He say, behold how the birds fly, which were a thing impossible to man; but that they are fed without taking thought, a kind of thing easy to be achieved by us also, if we will' (Homilies on Matthew 21).

EYE.title: God saw that it was good

left.text: and God saw that it was good.

right.text: And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good.

lines.text: The good-eye idea goes back to creation: God saw that what He made was good (Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21, 25), culminating in 'very good' (Genesis 1:31). The Jews of Jesus' day understood that because God has a good eye, they should too, in their dealings with each other.
The Hebrew tov (H2896), 'good,' is the word in the idiom 'good of eye.'

EYE.title: He who is generous will be blessed

src.text: He who is generous will be blessed, / For he gives from his food to the poor.

lines.text: In Hebrew, 'whoever has a good eye will be blessed.' If you have God's good eye, you are a generous person with a generous outlook on life. Psalm 18:25: God shows Himself merciful to the merciful.
The Hebrew reads tov-'ayin, literally 'good of eye.' The LSB translates the sense, 'generous.' The verse itself defines it: 'he gives from his food to the poor.'

left.text: Beware lest there be a vile thought in your heart, saying, ‘The seventh year, the year of the remission of debts, is near,’ and your eye is hostile toward your needy brother, and you give him nothing

right.text: A man with an evil eye hurries after wealth / And does not know that want will come upon him.

lines.text: The flip side: with a bad eye you look for the bad in the world and in other people, instead of beauty and potential. And you end up finding it.

In Scripture the 'evil eye' is above all stinginess: a hostile eye toward the needy (Deuteronomy 15:9), an eye that 'hurries after wealth' (Proverbs 28:22). Jesus uses the idiom later: 'Or is your eye envious because I am generous?' (Matthew 20:15), literally 'is your eye evil?'

EYE.title: A mighty man of valor, a man after His heart

left.text: Yahweh is with you, O mighty man of valor.

right.text: Yahweh has sought out for Himself a man after His own heart

lines.text: The good eye overlooks the flaw to see the value and potential in all people. That is why God can call a coward like Gideon 'a mighty man of valor,' and an adulterer and murderer like David 'a man after My heart.'
Gideon was hiding, threshing wheat in a wine press (Judges 6:11), when the angel called him valiant. Paul repeats God's words about David in Acts 13:22.

src.text: Therefore I speak to them in parables; because while seeing they do not see, and while hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand.

lines.text: Truly seeing with the eye becomes a recurring theme for Jesus. We'll highlight it as we read on.

src.text: Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind. And if a blind man guides a blind man, both will fall into a pit.

lines.text: These people could not see because they had a bad eye, and it caused them to miss the kingdom of heaven unfolding in front of them. The sermon's clash of disciples and Pharisees is, in one sense, a battle between the good eye and the bad eye.
In Matthew 23 Jesus calls the scribes and Pharisees blind five times: 'blind guides,' 'blind men,' 'blind Pharisee' (23:16, 17, 19, 24, 26).

PEOPLE.name: Jesus
PEOPLE.video: Gives His students both the what of the sermon and the how: have the Father's good eye.
PEOPLE.bg: Jesus Himself sees crowds with compassion, 'like sheep without a shepherd' (Matthew 9:36).

PEOPLE.name: The disciples, 'of little faith'
PEOPLE.video: They have families and responsibilities. How can they live without worry? Jesus anticipates the struggle.
PEOPLE.bg: 'You of little faith' (oligopistos) is a favorite word of Jesus in Matthew (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8).

PEOPLE.name: Solomon
PEOPLE.video: 'Not even Solomon in all his glory' was clothed like a wildflower.
PEOPLE.bg: Israel's richest king: 'greater than all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom' (1 Kings 10:23).

PEOPLE.name: Gideon
PEOPLE.video: A coward God called 'a mighty man of valor,' because God has a good eye.
PEOPLE.bg: He was threshing wheat in a wine press to hide it from the Midianites (Judges 6:11).

PEOPLE.name: David
PEOPLE.video: An adulterer and murderer God called 'a man after My heart.'
PEOPLE.bg: 1 Samuel 13:14 says it before David is anointed; Acts 13:22 repeats it.

PEOPLE.name: The Gentiles
PEOPLE.video: They 'eagerly seek' food, drink and clothing (6:32).
PEOPLE.bg: The same contrast as their prayers in 6:7-8: 'your Father knows what you need.'

TERMS.def: A Hebrew idiom for a generous, gracious outlook (Proverbs 22:9, literally 'good of eye'). The video's key to 6:22.
The opposite: stinginess, envy, a hostile eye toward the needy (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22; Matthew 20:15).
Wealth with God that cannot be lost: in Matthew, linked to generosity (19:21).
Money and possessions personified as a master that competes with God (6:24).
About 45 cm (18 in), forearm length. 'Add a single cubit to his life span' (6:27): length of life, or height.
Jesus' gentle rebuke for disciples who trust Him, but not enough (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8).
A mirrored pattern. The video sees 6:19-34 as the partner of the end of chapter 5, across the sermon's center (the Lord's Prayer).
Priority, not exclusion: 'His kingdom and His righteousness' first, and 'all these things will be added' (6:33).

WORDS.gloss: Moth, which eats fine cloth: a common form of wealth.
Eating, corrosion (LSB 'rust'): whatever eats away at stored goods.
Single, simple, sincere (LSB 'clear'). Related to haplotēs, 'generosity' (Romans 12:8). Look up: BDAG, ἁπλοῦς.
Bad, evil (LSB 'bad' in 6:23; 'envious' in 20:15, literally 'evil eye').
Wealth, property (from Aramaic): 'mammon.' Look up: BDAG, μαμωνᾶς.
To be anxious, worry: six times in 6:25-34.
Lily; probably a general word for wildflowers.
Eye; in idioms, outlook or attitude: a 'hostile' or 'evil' eye.
Good, pleasant, beneficial: 'God saw that it was good.' With 'ayin, 'good of eye' = generous.
Bad, evil; with 'ayin, 'evil eye' = stingy, grudging.

BACKGROUND.p: With no banks for ordinary people, wealth meant fine clothing, stored grain and buried coins: all open to moths, rot and thieves who 'break in' (literally 'dig through') mud-brick walls.

BACKGROUND.h: How eyes were thought to work
BACKGROUND.p: Many ancient writers thought the eye gave out light rather than only receiving it. Jesus' picture fits that world: the eye is a lamp; what kind of eye you have decides whether you are full of light or darkness.

BACKGROUND.h: The good eye and evil eye
BACKGROUND.p: Proverbs uses both phrases (22:9; 23:6; 28:22). Later Jewish teaching kept the idiom: the Mishnah lists 'a good eye' among the marks of Abraham's disciples and 'an evil eye' among Balaam's (Avot 5:19).

BACKGROUND.h: Lilies and grass in the oven
BACKGROUND.p: In spring the Galilean hills are covered with red anemones, poppies and other wildflowers. Dried grass and stalks were used as quick fuel for clay ovens: 'tomorrow is thrown into the furnace' (6:30).

WITNESSES.text: for just what the eye is to the body, the same is the mind to the soul.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 20, on 6:22-23. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain). Chrysostom reads the eye as the mind, blinded by love of wealth.

WITNESSES.text: The cleansing of the heart, then, is as it were the cleansing of the eye by which God is seen; and in keeping that single, there ought to be as great care as the dignity of the object demands
WITNESSES.src: On the Sermon on the Mount, Book 2. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 6 (public domain). Augustine reads the 'single' eye as an undivided heart.

DEBATES.p: Generous (the Hebrew good-eye idiom, as the video says); single-minded and undivided toward God (Augustine; the verse sits between 'treasure' and 'two masters'); or simply healthy, a picture of the mind (Chrysostom). The ideas overlap: an undivided heart is a generous one.

DEBATES.h: Does 6:19-34 mirror the end of chapter 5?
DEBATES.p: Part of the video's whole-sermon chiasm, which it offers as a proposal. Others read 6:19-7:12 as a series of sayings on trust and possessions, framed by 'the Law and the Prophets' (5:17; 7:12).
The word can mean stature (height) or age (life span). Most modern versions read life span; either way, worry adds nothing.
Suggestions include anemones, crocuses and wild lilies; the word probably covers wildflowers in general.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says Jesus explains the earthly treasure 'in verse 2'; it means 6:25 (food, drink, clothing). Likewise 'chapter 5:1 16' is 5:16.

The video says the Greek 'muddles' the Hebrew idiom. Matthew's haplous ('clear') has its own link to generosity: its noun haplotēs means generosity (Romans 12:8), so the Greek supports the video's point.
God called David 'a man after His own heart' in 1 Samuel 13:14, before David's adultery and murder; Acts 13:22 repeats it later. God's good eye toward David still stands.
Psalm 18:25 in the LSB reads 'With the kind You show Yourself kind'; 'merciful' is from other versions.

The good eye is one of several readings of 6:22 (see Where scholars differ). The video itself adds that this is not 'purely about having a good outlook on life'; regeneration by the Spirit and repentance underlie it.

QUESTIONS: Where is your treasure right now? What do your calendar and bank statement say about where your heart is?
Think of someone you find hard to love. What would it look like to see them with God's good eye, the way He saw Gideon?
The video says, 'You always end up finding what you're looking for.' Where are you looking for the bad, and finding it?
Which worry from 6:25-34 (food, drink, clothing, tomorrow) speaks to you most? What would 'seek first His kingdom' look like there?
How does a bad eye lead to fear, anxiety and loneliness? Have you seen that in yourself or in our culture?
The video asks how this lesson applies to you in your situation. Write one sentence.
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience, centered on the how: one of the keys to fulfilling the Sermon on the Mount and being God's kingdom spreaders is to have God's good eye, and to have it, people must trust in Him. Remember the center of the Lord's Prayer: 'on earth as it is in heaven.' If the Lord has a good eye toward His creation and we are to mirror Him on earth, so should we. The same lesson applies to you today; keep thinking about how it applies in your situation.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): the good eye in Proverbs 22:9 is practical: 'he gives from his food to the poor.' This week, practice it twice: thank God by name for one good thing you see in a difficult person, and give something away before you have time to worry about it.

# Matthew 6:19-34 Study Notes: The REAL Meaning Behind Jesus' Teaching on the EYE! (Matthew 6:19-34)

Channel: Every Word | Length: 21:28 | Series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 6:19-34: treasures in heaven, the eye as the lamp of the body, two masters, and do not worry: look at the birds and the lilies, and seek first His kingdom and His righteousness.
- It looks like several separate messages, but Jesus is unpacking ideas that run through the whole sermon. The scene has not changed: disciples, with the crowds listening.
- How can disciples live without worry when they have families and responsibilities? Jesus' answer: your heart (6:21) and your eye (6:22).
- 'If your eye is clear' reaches for a Hebrew idiom, the good eye (ayin tovah). God saw that what He made was good (Genesis 1). A good eye looks at people with complete love and sees beauty and potential, the way God called Gideon a mighty man of valor. 'He who is generous' in Proverbs 22:9 is literally 'good of eye.'
- In the video's chiasm, 6:19-34 parallels the end of chapter 5: 'be perfect' (5:48) is answered here. How do I love completely like the Father? Have the Father's good eye. A bad eye looks for the bad and finds it, leading to fear, anxiety and worry.
- The lesson: one key to fulfilling the sermon is to have God's good eye, and that takes trusting Him. The Pharisees had a bad eye and missed the kingdom in front of them. If the Lord has a good eye toward His creation and we mirror Him on earth as in heaven, so should we.

## Key quotes from the video (auto-captions, lightly cleaned)
> "Your heart must be guarded carefully because of what is inside of it."
> "To have God's good eye is to look at the world, to look around at people, from the perspective of complete love."
> "You always end up finding what you're looking for."
> "If we have God's good eye, we will find the beauty and the potential that we seek in others, which is the key to giving love."
> "One of the keys to fulfilling the Sermon on the Mount and being God's kingdom spreaders is to have God's good eye."

### Ask what holds the passage together
At first 6:19-34 looks like four separate sayings: treasure, the eye, two masters, worry. The teacher's question: what single idea joins them, and how do they connect back to chapter 5? Read the passage once looking for the word 'eye' and once looking for 'heart.'

## Key verses (LSB)
- "for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." (Matthew 6:21 (LSB))
- "The eye is the lamp of the body; so then if your eye is clear, your whole body will be full of light." (Matthew 6:22 (LSB))
- "But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." (Matthew 6:33 (LSB))

## Treasure, eye, masters, worry
1. Treasure · Matthew 6:19-21: Where your treasure is
   Heart Matthew 6:19-21: "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal; for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+6:19-21
   (video) The earthly treasure is food, drink and clothes (6:25). All of it will disappear: moth, rust and thieves. Instead God's people focus on His kingdom and His righteousness, different from the righteousness of the religious leaders.
   [Background] 'Destroy' (aphanizō) is the same verb as the fasters who 'neglect their appearance' in 6:16. 'Rust' is literally 'eating' (brōsis). Luke adds: 'Sell your possessions and give it as charity' (Luke 12:33). (Luke 12:33-34; Proverbs 23:4-5)
2. The eye · Matthew 6:22-23: The eye is the lamp of the body
   Good eye Matthew 6:22-23: "The eye is the lamp of the body; so then if your eye is clear, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+6:22-23
   (video) My translation says 'healthy,' but Jesus is reaching for something very Jewish: the good eye. If your heart is wrong, your focus will be off; if your eye is not good, you'll end up serving what you should not.
   [Background] 'Clear' is haplous (G573): single, sincere. Its noun haplotēs means generosity: 'he who gives, with generosity' (Romans 12:8). 'Bad' is ponēros, 'evil,' as in the 'evil eye' of stinginess. (Romans 12:8)
3. Two masters · Matthew 6:24: God or wealth
   Choose Matthew 6:24: "No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+6:24
   (video) The disciple faces a choice, and Jesus is the one forcing it. It all comes down to which eye you choose to have.
   [Background] 'Serve' is douleuō, to serve as a slave. 'Wealth' is mamōnas, an Aramaic word for money and property (older versions: 'mammon'). The evil eye 'hurries after wealth' (Proverbs 28:22). (Proverbs 28:22)
4. Worry · Matthew 6:25-34: Look at the birds, observe the lilies
   The birds (Matthew 6:26, LSB): "Look at the birds of the air, that they do not sow, nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?"
   The lilies (Matthew 6:28-29, LSB): "Observe how the lilies of the field grow; they do not toil nor do they spin, yet I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory clothed himself like one of these."
   (video) A bad eye looks for things to fear and mistrust, and finds them; that leads to anxiety, worry and loneliness. That is why Jesus moves from the eye straight to worry.
   [Background] God 'gives to the animal its food, / And to the young ravens which call out' (Psalm 147:9). 'All flesh is grass' (Isaiah 40:6). The answer to worry is a priority: 'seek first His kingdom' (6:33). (Psalm 147:9; Isaiah 40:6-8; Philippians 4:6-7)
   Chrysostom: 'For neither did He say, behold how the birds fly, which were a thing impossible to man; but that they are fed without taking thought, a kind of thing easy to be achieved by us also, if we will' (Homilies on Matthew 21).

## The Father's good eye
1. God's good eye · Genesis 1: God saw that it was good
   Day three (Genesis 1:10, LSB): "and God saw that it was good."
   Day six (Genesis 1:31, LSB): "And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good."
   (video) The good-eye idea goes back to creation: God saw that what He made was good (Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21, 25), culminating in 'very good' (Genesis 1:31). The Jews of Jesus' day understood that because God has a good eye, they should too, in their dealings with each other.
   [Background] The Hebrew tov (H2896), 'good,' is the word in the idiom 'good of eye.' (Genesis 1:12; Genesis 1:25)
2. The good eye · Proverbs 22:9: He who is generous will be blessed
   Ayin tovah Proverbs 22:9: "He who is generous will be blessed, / For he gives from his food to the poor." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Proverbs+22:9
   (video) In Hebrew, 'whoever has a good eye will be blessed.' If you have God's good eye, you are a generous person with a generous outlook on life. Psalm 18:25: God shows Himself merciful to the merciful. (Psalm 18:25)
   [Background] The Hebrew reads tov-'ayin, literally 'good of eye.' The LSB translates the sense, 'generous.' The verse itself defines it: 'he gives from his food to the poor.'
3. The bad eye · Deuteronomy 15; Proverbs 28: An evil eye
   Moses (Deuteronomy 15:9, LSB): "Beware lest there be a vile thought in your heart, saying, ‘The seventh year, the year of the remission of debts, is near,’ and your eye is hostile toward your needy brother, and you give him nothing"
   Proverbs (Proverbs 28:22, LSB): "A man with an evil eye hurries after wealth / And does not know that want will come upon him."
   (video) The flip side: with a bad eye you look for the bad in the world and in other people, instead of beauty and potential. And you end up finding it.
   [Background] In Scripture the 'evil eye' is above all stinginess: a hostile eye toward the needy (Deuteronomy 15:9), an eye that 'hurries after wealth' (Proverbs 28:22). Jesus uses the idiom later: 'Or is your eye envious because I am generous?' (Matthew 20:15), literally 'is your eye evil?' (Matthew 20:1-16; Proverbs 23:6)
4. Seeing potential · Judges 6; 1 Samuel 13: A mighty man of valor, a man after His heart
   To Gideon (Judges 6:12, LSB): "Yahweh is with you, O mighty man of valor."
   Of David (1 Samuel 13:14, LSB): "Yahweh has sought out for Himself a man after His own heart"
   (video) The good eye overlooks the flaw to see the value and potential in all people. That is why God can call a coward like Gideon 'a mighty man of valor,' and an adulterer and murderer like David 'a man after My heart.'
   [Background] Gideon was hiding, threshing wheat in a wine press (Judges 6:11), when the angel called him valiant. Paul repeats God's words about David in Acts 13:22. (Judges 6:11; Acts 13:22)

## Seeing and not seeing
1. A recurring theme · Matthew 13: Seeing, they do not see
   Later Matthew 13:13: "Therefore I speak to them in parables; because while seeing they do not see, and while hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+13:13
   (video) Truly seeing with the eye becomes a recurring theme for Jesus. We'll highlight it as we read on.
2. The bad eye · Matthew 15: Blind guides of the blind
   Later Matthew 15:14: "Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind. And if a blind man guides a blind man, both will fall into a pit." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+15:14
   (video) These people could not see because they had a bad eye, and it caused them to miss the kingdom of heaven unfolding in front of them. The sermon's clash of disciples and Pharisees is, in one sense, a battle between the good eye and the bad eye.
   [Background] In Matthew 23 Jesus calls the scribes and Pharisees blind five times: 'blind guides,' 'blind men,' 'blind Pharisee' (23:16, 17, 19, 24, 26). (Matthew 23:16-26)

## Key people
- Jesus: Gives His students both the what of the sermon and the how: have the Father's good eye. [Background] Jesus Himself sees crowds with compassion, 'like sheep without a shepherd' (Matthew 9:36).
- The disciples, 'of little faith': They have families and responsibilities. How can they live without worry? Jesus anticipates the struggle. [Background] 'You of little faith' (oligopistos) is a favorite word of Jesus in Matthew (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8).
- Solomon: 'Not even Solomon in all his glory' was clothed like a wildflower. [Background] Israel's richest king: 'greater than all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom' (1 Kings 10:23).
- Gideon: A coward God called 'a mighty man of valor,' because God has a good eye. [Background] He was threshing wheat in a wine press to hide it from the Midianites (Judges 6:11).
- David: An adulterer and murderer God called 'a man after My heart.' [Background] 1 Samuel 13:14 says it before David is anointed; Acts 13:22 repeats it.
- The Gentiles: They 'eagerly seek' food, drink and clothing (6:32). [Background] The same contrast as their prayers in 6:7-8: 'your Father knows what you need.'

## Places [Background]
- Arbel: Cliffs and fields where red anemones bloom each spring (photo below). Many guess the 'lilies of the field' were wildflowers like these.
- Plain of Gennesaret: A fertile plain on the northwest shore, famous for its crops: fields, barns and harvest close at hand.
- Mount of Beatitudes: The traditional site of the sermon.
- Capernaum: Jesus' home base by the lake (4:13).
- Magdala: A prosperous fishing town: storehouses, nets and trade.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital with its royal palace, a picture of earthly 'glory.'
- Bethsaida: Home town of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44).
- Hippos: A Gentile city across the lake (compare 'the Gentiles eagerly seek,' 6:32).

## Key terms
- Good eye (ayin tovah): A Hebrew idiom for a generous, gracious outlook (Proverbs 22:9, literally 'good of eye'). The video's key to 6:22.
- Evil eye (ayin ra'ah): The opposite: stinginess, envy, a hostile eye toward the needy (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22; Matthew 20:15). [Background]
- Treasure in heaven: Wealth with God that cannot be lost: in Matthew, linked to generosity (19:21). [Background]
- Wealth (mammon): Money and possessions personified as a master that competes with God (6:24). [Background]
- Cubit: About 45 cm (18 in), forearm length. 'Add a single cubit to his life span' (6:27): length of life, or height. [Background]
- Little faith: Jesus' gentle rebuke for disciples who trust Him, but not enough (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8). [Background]
- Chiasm: A mirrored pattern. The video sees 6:19-34 as the partner of the end of chapter 5, across the sermon's center (the Lord's Prayer).
- Seek first: Priority, not exclusion: 'His kingdom and His righteousness' first, and 'all these things will be added' (6:33). [Background]

## Hebrew and Greek words [Background; Strong's numbers follow the LSB's word tagging]
- θησαυρός thēsauros (G2344, Greek): Treasure, storehouse (our 'thesaurus'). (Matt 6:19, 20, 21)
- σής sēs (G4597, Greek): Moth, which eats fine cloth: a common form of wealth. (Matt 6:19, 20)
- βρῶσις brōsis (G1035, Greek): Eating, corrosion (LSB 'rust'): whatever eats away at stored goods. (Matt 6:19, 20)
- ἁπλοῦς haplous (G573, Greek): Single, simple, sincere (LSB 'clear'). Related to haplotēs, 'generosity' (Romans 12:8). Look up: BDAG, ἁπλοῦς. (Matt 6:22)
- ἁπλότης haplotēs (G572, Greek): Simplicity, sincerity, generosity. (Rom 12:8)
- πονηρός ponēros (G4190, Greek): Bad, evil (LSB 'bad' in 6:23; 'envious' in 20:15, literally 'evil eye'). (Matt 6:23; 20:15)
- δουλεύω douleuō (G1398, Greek): To serve as a slave. (Matt 6:24)
- μαμωνᾶς mamōnas (G3126, Greek): Wealth, property (from Aramaic): 'mammon.' Look up: BDAG, μαμωνᾶς. (Matt 6:24)
- μεριμνάω merimnaō (G3309, Greek): To be anxious, worry: six times in 6:25-34. (Matt 6:25, 27, 28, 34)
- κρίνον krinon (G2918, Greek): Lily; probably a general word for wildflowers. (Matt 6:28)
- ὀλιγόπιστος oligopistos (G3640, Greek): Of little faith. (Matt 6:30)
- ζητέω zēteō (G2212, Greek): To seek, strive for. (Matt 6:33)
- עַיִן 'ayin (H5869, Hebrew): Eye; in idioms, outlook or attitude: a 'hostile' or 'evil' eye. (Deut 15:9; Prov 28:22)
- טוֹב tov (H2896, Hebrew): Good, pleasant, beneficial: 'God saw that it was good.' With 'ayin, 'good of eye' = generous. (Gen 1:31)
- רַע ra' (H7451, Hebrew): Bad, evil; with 'ayin, 'evil eye' = stingy, grudging. (Prov 28:22)

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Wealth in the ancient world: With no banks for ordinary people, wealth meant fine clothing, stored grain and buried coins: all open to moths, rot and thieves who 'break in' (literally 'dig through') mud-brick walls.
- How eyes were thought to work: Many ancient writers thought the eye gave out light rather than only receiving it. Jesus' picture fits that world: the eye is a lamp; what kind of eye you have decides whether you are full of light or darkness.
- The good eye and evil eye: Proverbs uses both phrases (22:9; 23:6; 28:22). Later Jewish teaching kept the idiom: the Mishnah lists 'a good eye' among the marks of Abraham's disciples and 'an evil eye' among Balaam's (Avot 5:19).
- Lilies and grass in the oven: In spring the Galilean hills are covered with red anemones, poppies and other wildflowers. Dried grass and stalks were used as quick fuel for clay ovens: 'tomorrow is thrown into the furnace' (6:30).

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "for just what the eye is to the body, the same is the mind to the soul." Homilies on Matthew 20, on 6:22-23. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain). Chrysostom reads the eye as the mind, blinded by love of wealth.
- Augustine of Hippo (c. AD 393): "The cleansing of the heart, then, is as it were the cleansing of the eye by which God is seen; and in keeping that single, there ought to be as great care as the dignity of the object demands" On the Sermon on the Mount, Book 2. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 6 (public domain). Augustine reads the 'single' eye as an undivided heart.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- What is a 'clear' eye? Generous (the Hebrew good-eye idiom, as the video says); single-minded and undivided toward God (Augustine; the verse sits between 'treasure' and 'two masters'); or simply healthy, a picture of the mind (Chrysostom). The ideas overlap: an undivided heart is a generous one.
- Does 6:19-34 mirror the end of chapter 5? Part of the video's whole-sermon chiasm, which it offers as a proposal. Others read 6:19-7:12 as a series of sayings on trust and possessions, framed by 'the Law and the Prophets' (5:17; 7:12).
- 'A cubit to his life span' The word can mean stature (height) or age (life span). Most modern versions read life span; either way, worry adds nothing.
- What were the 'lilies'? Suggestions include anemones, crocuses and wild lilies; the word probably covers wildflowers in general.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says Jesus explains the earthly treasure 'in verse 2'; it means 6:25 (food, drink, clothing). Likewise 'chapter 5:1 16' is 5:16.
- The video says the Greek 'muddles' the Hebrew idiom. Matthew's haplous ('clear') has its own link to generosity: its noun haplotēs means generosity (Romans 12:8), so the Greek supports the video's point.
- God called David 'a man after His own heart' in 1 Samuel 13:14, before David's adultery and murder; Acts 13:22 repeats it later. God's good eye toward David still stands.
- Psalm 18:25 in the LSB reads 'With the kind You show Yourself kind'; 'merciful' is from other versions.
- The good eye is one of several readings of 6:22 (see Where scholars differ). The video itself adds that this is not 'purely about having a good outlook on life'; regeneration by the Spirit and repentance underlie it.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Where is your treasure right now? What do your calendar and bank statement say about where your heart is?
2. Think of someone you find hard to love. What would it look like to see them with God's good eye, the way He saw Gideon?
3. The video says, 'You always end up finding what you're looking for.' Where are you looking for the bad, and finding it?
4. Which worry from 6:25-34 (food, drink, clothing, tomorrow) speaks to you most? What would 'seek first His kingdom' look like there?
5. How does a bad eye lead to fear, anxiety and loneliness? Have you seen that in yourself or in our culture?
6. The video asks how this lesson applies to you in your situation. Write one sentence.

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience, centered on the how: one of the keys to fulfilling the Sermon on the Mount and being God's kingdom spreaders is to have God's good eye, and to have it, people must trust in Him. Remember the center of the Lord's Prayer: 'on earth as it is in heaven.' If the Lord has a good eye toward His creation and we are to mirror Him on earth, so should we. The same lesson applies to you today; keep thinking about how it applies in your situation.
- Study note (added): the good eye in Proverbs 22:9 is practical: 'he gives from his food to the poor.' This week, practice it twice: thank God by name for one good thing you see in a difficult person, and give something away before you have time to worry about it.
